case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Title III of the Helms‑Burton Act (LIBERTAD Act) imposes civil liability on a defendant who ‘traffics’ in confiscated Cuban property when the defendant’s use of the property occurs after the plaintiff acquires ownership of the claim, or whether the plaintiff must have owned the claim at the time the defendant began/engaged in the trafficking conduct.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Title III of the Cuban Liberty and Democratic Solidarity (LIBERTAD) Act of 1996 (Helms‑Burton Act), 22 U.S.C. § 6082(a)(1)(A) (private right of action for U.S. nationals who own a claim to confiscated property against any person who traffics in such property), along with Title III’s definitions/limitations including the definition of “traffics in” in 22 U.S.C. § 6023(13) and related provisions governing who may sue and damages.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Havana Docks argues that the text and structure of Title III allow suit so long as (1) the plaintiff is a U.S. national who owns the claim when the action is filed and (2) the defendant traffics in the confiscated property during the actionable period; the statute does not require the plaintiff to have owned the claim when the defendant’s trafficking first began or to show a contemporaneous match between initial trafficking and claim ownership. Petitioner contends the Eleventh Circuit effectively added an extra-statutory timing/ownership requirement that narrows Congress’s chosen remedy, undermines deterrence, and frustrates Title III’s foreign-policy and compensation purposes (a view supported by the United States as amicus, which emphasizes Congress’s intent to create an effective mechanism to deter collaboration with the Cuban regime and compensate victims of confiscation).
case_analysis.respondent_position: The cruise-line respondents argue that Title III should be read to require a tighter nexus between the plaintiff’s ownership and the trafficking conduct—i.e., that a plaintiff cannot sue based on trafficking that predates the plaintiff’s acquisition of the claim (and, in their view, the Eleventh Circuit correctly limited liability accordingly). They emphasize limiting principles to avoid expansive retroactive-like liability and to prevent creating a sweeping, unpredictable cause of action affecting travel and commerce. Respondents and their supporting amici (travel industry groups and cruise industry association) frame petitioner’s interpretation as overbroad and destabilizing, potentially exposing routine travel-related activity to massive damages and complicating foreign-relations sensitivities embedded in Congress’s enforcement design (including the statute’s historically suspended activation).

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Alito’s Landgraf-based concern is substantial, but it depends on treating the plaintiff’s later acquisition of a claim as creating liability for “completed past conduct.” As Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, § 6082(a)(1)(A) is written in present-tense predicates (plaintiff “owns the claim,” defendant “traffics in”), and § 6023(13) defines trafficking as ongoing “use/benefit” conduct, so we can avoid any retroactivity problem by limiting liability to trafficking occurring after Title III became operative and during the period the plaintiff owns the claim. Congress also included express timing limits elsewhere (as Justice Kavanaugh notes, e.g., § 6082(a)(4)(B)), which under a minimalist, text-bound approach counsels against judicially grafting an additional “ownership-at-commencement” requirement onto silence. A narrow holding on those points—without pronouncing broadly on foreign-relations consequences—best respects precedent, preserves institutional legitimacy, and applies the statute as written.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Alito’s Landgraf-based objection is the best counter, but it still asks us to graft onto § 6082(a)(1)(A) a contemporaneous-ownership-at-inception requirement Congress did not enact. As the Chief Justice and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, the operative text uses present-tense predicates—plaintiff “owns the claim” and defendant “traffics in” the property—and § 6023(13) defines trafficking as ongoing “use,” “management,” or “benefit,” so liability may be confined to post-effective-date, post-acquisition trafficking without attaching new consequences to completed past acts. Landgraf’s presumption against retroactivity cannot justify rewriting a clear cause of action, especially where Congress elsewhere supplied express timing limitations (e.g., § 6082(a)(4)(B)), underscoring that silence here is not an invitation for judicial supplementation. Policy concerns about destabilizing settled arrangements are real, but under an originalist, textualist approach they are for Congress to address, not this Court.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: I appreciate the Chief Justice’s and Justice Thomas’s point that § 6082(a)(1)(A) is drafted in present-tense terms and that Congress included explicit timing limits elsewhere, but that does not answer the Landgraf problem I am flagging. Even if we confine damages to post-effective-date “traffics in” conduct, the broad, continuous definition of “traffics” in § 6023(13) allows a later-acquiring plaintiff to transform an ongoing commercial relationship—initiated when that plaintiff had no enforceable right—into actionable exposure, which has the same destabilizing, retroactive-like effect Landgraf cautions against absent a clear statement. Justice Kagan’s proposed narrowing (damages only during plaintiff’s ownership) still permits bootstrapping by claim purchasers and invites strategic transfers to manufacture standing against established operations, a practical consequence I do not think Congress silently embraced in this carefully cabined remedial scheme. Because the statute is at least ambiguous on this timing question, I would read it to require ownership of the claim at the inception of the challenged trafficking course to avoid imposing unexpected liability through later claim acquisition.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito’s retroactivity-like concern is serious, but it still depends on recharacterizing the operative event: Title III imposes liability for a defendant’s ongoing choice to “traffic,” and § 6082(a)(1)(A) asks in the present tense whether the plaintiff “owns the claim” when bringing suit. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Landgraf is satisfied so long as we cabin liability to trafficking occurring after Title III became operative and after the plaintiff’s acquisition—so we are not attaching new consequences to completed past conduct, but regulating continuing commercial exploitation that the defendant can stop. Alito’s proposed “ownership-at-commencement-of-trafficking” rule is not a limiting construction drawn from text; it is an extra statutory hurdle that would predictably fall hardest on families and individuals who often obtain or perfect claims later and would undercut Congress’s deterrent design. The administrable line is the one Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh identify: damages keyed to actionable-period trafficking, which avoids unfair surprise without judicially narrowing the remedy Congress enacted.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Alito’s Landgraf-based objection is the best argument for Respondent, but it still treats the “past conduct” as the plaintiff’s later acquisition of a claim rather than the defendant’s present-tense, ongoing “traffics in” conduct as defined in § 6023(13) (continued “use,” “manage,” or “benefit from”). As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, § 6082(a)(1)(A) sets two textual predicates—plaintiff “owns the claim” and defendant “traffics”—and Congress knew how to add explicit timing limits elsewhere, so grafting a commencement-of-trafficking ownership rule would be an atextual narrowing. Landgraf’s concern about attaching new consequences to completed conduct is satisfied by limiting liability and damages to trafficking occurring after Title III is operative and during the period the plaintiff owns the claim, which preserves statutory coherence and a workable line without rewriting the cause of action. Alito’s policy concern about destabilizing reliance interests is real, but under a pragmatic textualist approach it cannot override the statute’s enacted structure when prospective liability can be cleanly confined to ongoing conduct.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Alito’s Landgraf-based concern identifies a real risk of attaching new consequences to earlier-initiated conduct, but it still asks us to graft a contemporaneous-ownership-at-commencement rule onto § 6082(a)(1)(A) that Congress did not enact. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas emphasize, the operative predicates are written in the present tense—plaintiff “owns the claim” and defendant “traffics in” the property—and § 6023(13) frames trafficking as ongoing “use” or “benefit from,” so liability can be confined to post-effective-date, post-acquisition trafficking without regulating completed past acts. Alito’s “bootstrapping” worry is ultimately a policy objection about expanded exposure; under a textualist methodology, that concern cannot justify narrowing clear statutory language, especially where Congress elsewhere added explicit timing limits (e.g., § 6082(a)(4)(B)). I therefore remain with Petitioner, with the administrable limitation that damages attach only to trafficking during the period when Title III is operative and the plaintiff owns the claim.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Alito’s retroactivity concern is serious, but it still mislocates the Landgraf inquiry: the statute’s liability attaches to the defendant’s trafficking during the actionable period, not to the historical confiscation or the defendant’s earlier initiation of a course of dealing. As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, § 6082(a)(1)(A) sets present-tense predicates—plaintiff “owns the claim” and defendant “traffics”—and Congress’s inclusion of explicit timing limits elsewhere (e.g., § 6082(a)(4)(B)) undercuts judicially implying an additional ownership-at-commencement bar. The administrable, institutionally modest answer is to confine damages to post-effective-date trafficking that occurs while the plaintiff owns the claim, which addresses Alito’s destabilization worries without rewriting the statute. Under my precedent-and-text methodology, adding Alito’s contemporaneous-ownership rule would be atextual and unnecessary to avoid retroactive attachment of new legal consequences to completed past conduct.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Alito’s Landgraf-based retroactivity concern is substantial, but it relies on importing a plaintiff-ownership-at-commencement requirement that the text of § 6082(a)(1)(A) does not contain. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, Landgraf asks whether the statute attaches new legal consequences to completed past conduct; a liability rule limited to post-effective-date, post-acquisition “traffics in” conduct (as defined in § 6023(13) through ongoing verbs like “uses” and “benefits from”) regulates present conduct and avoids retroactive attachment. The fact that Congress expressly wrote other timing constraints (e.g., § 6082(a)(4)(B))—a point pressed by Justice Gorsuch—cuts strongly against judicially grafting an additional temporality limitation onto silence. On an originalist, textualist reading, the administrable line is to require ownership at suit and tie damages to trafficking during the period of qualified ownership, not to rewrite the cause of action to address policy concerns better left to Congress.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Alito’s Landgraf-based “retroactive-like” concern is the best argument for Respondent, but it still depends on treating the plaintiff’s later acquisition as the operative event that makes earlier conduct newly actionable; the statute instead keys liability to the defendant’s present-tense “traffics in” conduct, which § 6023(13) defines as ongoing “use” or “benefit from.” As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Sotomayor stress, we can avoid any genuine retroactivity problem by tethering liability and damages to post-effective-date, post-ownership trafficking—i.e., to the defendant’s continuing choices—without grafting an extra-textual contemporaneous-ownership-at-commencement requirement onto § 6082(a)(1)(A). Procedural fairness is better served by that administrable line because it gives defendants a clear way to avoid liability (stop trafficking once the claim exists and the statute is operative) while preserving Congress’s remedial design for victims. Alito’s destabilization concern is ultimately a policy argument about the breadth of Title III, and given Congress’s explicit timing limits elsewhere, it does not justify judicially narrowing a cause of action whose text already supplies workable temporal boundaries.

John Roberts.reasoning: Title III’s cause of action turns on whether, at the time suit is brought, the plaintiff “owns the claim” and the defendant “traffics in such property,” 22 U.S.C. § 6082(a)(1)(A); it does not textually require that the plaintiff have owned the claim when the defendant’s trafficking first began. Reading in that additional temporal-ownership limitation would narrow Congress’s chosen remedial scheme and is difficult to square with Title III’s focus on ongoing “traffics in” conduct as defined in § 6023(13) (which encompasses continued “use” and “benefit” from confiscated property). Properly understood, applying liability only to post-acquisition trafficking (even if the defendant’s course of conduct began earlier) does not raise the retroactivity concerns addressed in Landgraf because the statute is being applied to post-acquisition, post-effective-date conduct rather than attaching new legal consequences to completed past acts. A narrow holding on these statutory grounds respects precedent, avoids unnecessary foreign-relations broadside, and preserves the Court’s institutional role by enforcing the statute as written.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of Title III imposes liability on any person who “traffics in property which was confiscated by the Cuban Government,” and grants a cause of action to “any United States national who owns the claim to such property,” 22 U.S.C. § 6082(a)(1)(A); it does not add a requirement that the plaintiff must have owned the claim when the defendant’s trafficking first began. Congress elsewhere supplied explicit timing limits (e.g., the pre-1996 acquisition bar in § 6082(a)(4)(B) and the statutory definition of “traffics” in § 6023(13)), so it is not this Court’s role to graft an extra-statutory contemporaneity condition onto § 6082(a)(1)(A). Properly read, liability turns on trafficking conduct occurring during the actionable period and the plaintiff’s ownership of the claim at suit, and this construction does not offend the presumption against retroactivity because it attaches consequences to post-effective-date trafficking rather than pre-enactment conduct. Under Landgraf v. USI Film Products, 511 U.S. 244 (1994), courts should not manufacture retroactivity concerns to rewrite clear statutory text, particularly where Congress targeted ongoing commercial use of confiscated property.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Title III’s cause of action turns on whether the defendant "traffics" in confiscated property, 22 U.S.C. § 6082(a)(1)(A), but the statute should not be read to impose sweeping liability untethered to the plaintiff’s ownership of the claim at the time the challenged course of conduct began. Absent a clear statement, we apply the presumption against retroactivity to avoid attaching new civil consequences to conduct that, at the time it commenced, did not expose the defendant to suit by this plaintiff—an approach consistent with Landgraf v. USI Film Products, 511 U.S. 244 (1994). Reading Title III to allow later-acquired claims to generate liability for earlier-initiated trafficking would expand exposure in a destabilizing, retroactive-like way that Congress did not clearly authorize, especially given Title III’s careful limitations (including who may sue and damages) and the practical consequences for commerce and foreign relations. Accordingly, a plaintiff must have owned the claim when the relevant trafficking conduct began (or at least when the actionable trafficking giving rise to liability first occurred), and later acquisition cannot bootstrap liability for antecedent trafficking activity.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Title III’s text imposes liability on “any person that … traffics in property which was confiscated … to which the United States national owns the claim,” 22 U.S.C. § 6082(a)(1)(A), tying the ownership requirement to the plaintiff’s status when suing, not to the defendant’s first act of trafficking. The Eleventh Circuit’s added requirement that the plaintiff must have owned the claim when the trafficking began lacks textual footing and undermines Congress’s remedial design to deter ongoing commercial use of confiscated property and to prioritize certified claimholders (including enhanced damages and evidentiary presumptions for certified claims). Nor does this interpretation create impermissible retroactivity under Landgraf v. USI Film Products because liability attaches to post-effective-date/post-acquisition trafficking (a defendant’s continuing conduct), even if the underlying confiscation or earlier use predates the plaintiff’s acquisition. Reading the statute to cover ongoing trafficking better serves fairness and access to justice for victims of expropriation—often those least able to vindicate their rights—while still limiting liability to defendants who choose to engage in trafficking during the actionable period.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Title III’s cause of action turns on two textual predicates: the plaintiff must “own[] the claim to such property” and the defendant must “traffic[] in such property.” 22 U.S.C. § 6082(a)(1)(A). The statute defines “traffics” in conduct-based terms—e.g., “uses,” “manages,” or “otherwise acquires or holds an interest in confiscated property,” 22 U.S.C. § 6023(13)—so liability attaches to post-acquisition trafficking conduct without an extra, judicially invented requirement that the plaintiff have owned the claim when the trafficking first began. Reading in that additional timing limitation is hard to square with Congress’s workable design (including ongoing-use verbs) and with the general retroactivity framework of Landgraf, which asks whether the statute attaches new legal consequences to past conduct; here, the actionable trigger is the defendant’s post-ownership conduct, not the defendant’s earlier history with the property. That construction preserves statutory coherence and avoids unnecessary narrowing of the remedy Congress chose while still confining liability to trafficking that occurs during the relevant actionable period.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The statute’s text ties liability to a defendant who “traffics in property which was confiscated” and authorizes suit by “any United States national who owns the claim to such property” against “any person that … traffics in such property.” 22 U.S.C. § 6082(a)(1)(A). Nothing in Title III adds the extra requirement that the plaintiff must have owned the claim when the defendant’s trafficking first began; the ownership condition is stated in the present tense as a qualification to sue, while trafficking is defined as ongoing conduct (including “use” and “benefit from”) in § 6023(13), making post-acquisition trafficking actionable so long as the plaintiff owns the claim when suing. Reading in a commencement-of-trafficking timing rule would depart from the plain meaning and structure Congress enacted and would be especially suspect where it narrows a congressionally created cause of action without textual warrant. Nor does Landgraf compel respondents’ limitation: imposing liability only for post-activation/post-acquisition trafficking does not attach new legal consequences to completed past conduct; it regulates and provides remedies for conduct occurring after the statute is operative and the plaintiff is a qualified claimant.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Title III’s operative language imposes liability on “any person that … traffics in property which was confiscated by the Cuban Government” and creates a cause of action for any U.S. national who “owns the claim to such property,” 22 U.S.C. § 6082(a)(1)(A); the statute’s timing focus is on claim-ownership at suit and on the defendant’s trafficking during the actionable period, not on whether the plaintiff owned the claim when the trafficking first began. Reading an additional contemporaneous-ownership requirement into § 6082(a)(1)(A) lacks textual support and conflicts with the statute’s definition of “traffics” in § 6023(13), which covers ongoing “use” and “benefit” from confiscated property and thus naturally reaches post-acquisition conduct. The presumption against retroactivity, as articulated in Landgraf v. USI Film Products, is not triggered by petitioner’s reading because liability attaches only to trafficking occurring after Title III became effective as to defendants, not to pre-enactment conduct; the question here is about the plaintiff’s acquisition date, and Congress did not condition liability on the plaintiff having held the claim at the inception of the defendant’s course of conduct. That construction is also more workable and consistent with Congress’s structured limitations (e.g., who may sue and damages provisions) rather than atextual judicial narrowing in the name of policy concerns.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 6082(a)(1)(A) creates liability for “any person that … traffics in property which was confiscated,” and authorizes suit by a U.S. national who “owns the claim to such property”; the text ties the plaintiff’s status to ownership at the time of suit, not to the date the defendant’s trafficking first began. The definition of “traffics” in § 6023(13) describes a course of conduct (using, transferring, profiting from, etc.), so a defendant who continues that conduct after the plaintiff acquires the claim commits actionable trafficking during the period of the plaintiff’s ownership without any extra-statutory “contemporaneity” requirement. Reading in a rule that the plaintiff must have owned the claim when the defendant’s trafficking commenced adds a limitation Congress did not include, and the presumption against retroactivity in Landgraf v. USI Film Products is not triggered where liability is premised on post-acquisition conduct rather than attaching new consequences solely to completed past acts. Precedent and methodological consistency counsel adhering to the statute’s enacted timing and definitional choices rather than narrowing the cause of action based on policy concerns better addressed to Congress.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Title III’s cause of action turns on whether a defendant “traffics in property which was confiscated” and whether the plaintiff “owns the claim to such property” at the time it brings suit. 22 U.S.C. § 6082(a)(1)(A). The statute’s definition of “traffics” in 22 U.S.C. § 6023(13) focuses on the defendant’s use/benefit from the confiscated property, not on when the plaintiff first acquired its claim, and nothing in the text adds a requirement that the plaintiff must have owned the claim when the defendant’s trafficking began. Reading in such a timing bar would narrow Congress’s remedial design and undermine the practical deterrent/compensatory function of Title III without clear statutory command, while Landgraf’s retroactivity framework counsels focusing the statute’s “temporal reach” on the conduct that triggers liability (post-acquisition trafficking here) rather than on antecedent historical facts like when the claim was acquired. On this reading, liability properly attaches to trafficking occurring after the plaintiff owns the claim, preserving procedural fairness by tying damages to actionable-period conduct rather than imposing liability for entirely completed past acts.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Title III of the LIBERTAD (Helms-Burton) Act requires a plaintiff to prove that a defendant knowingly and intentionally trafficked in confiscated Cuban property (i.e., a freestanding scienter element), or whether liability turns primarily on the statute’s definition of “traffics,” including its knowledge-related carveouts and notice provisions.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Title III of the Cuban Liberty and Democratic Solidarity (LIBERTAD) Act of 1996 (Helms-Burton Act), 22 U.S.C. § 6082(a)(1)(A) (cause of action for U.S. nationals owning claims to confiscated property against any person who “traffics” in such property), and the statute’s definition and limitations concerning “traffics” in 22 U.S.C. § 6023(13) (including exclusions tied to knowledge/reason to know).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Havana Docks argues the Eleventh Circuit improperly added an atextual scienter requirement to Title III by demanding proof that the cruise lines subjectively knew and intended to traffic in confiscated property as an element of the cause of action. In petitioner’s view, Congress made a deliberate choice to impose broad civil liability on ‘any person’ who ‘traffics in’ confiscated property, while placing knowledge concepts where Congress wanted them—principally in the statutory definition of ‘traffics’ and its express exclusions/carveouts (e.g., exceptions for certain transactions when a person lacked and had no reason to know of the confiscation). Petitioner contends the lower court’s heightened mens rea rule undermines Congress’s deterrent purpose and frustrates Title III’s remedial scheme, especially because defendants can often avoid liability by structuring operations through intermediaries while plaintiffs lack access to internal corporate knowledge before discovery.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The cruise line respondents argue Title III should be read to incorporate a meaningful scienter requirement (at least knowledge, and in their framing often knowledge plus intent) before imposing potentially massive liability for commercial activity involving Cuban facilities. They contend that the ordinary meaning of ‘traffics’ and the structure of the Act signal Congress did not intend strict liability for routine commercial conduct where the defendant did not knowingly exploit confiscated property, and that the Eleventh Circuit’s approach best aligns with principles of fair notice, extraterritoriality/foreign-relations sensitivity, and avoiding sweeping liability that could chill lawful travel and commerce. Respondents also emphasize practical and policy concerns raised by the travel and cruise industry amici: that a low-threshold liability rule would expose broad swaths of travel-related businesses (including tour operators and travel advisors) to litigation risk and would destabilize the framework governing U.S.-Cuba travel, especially where companies rely on governmental authorizations and complex factual predicates about ownership and confiscation history.

John Roberts.reasoning: The respondent’s best argument remains the presumption of scienter and the fair-notice concern, but in this statute Congress already addressed that problem by embedding knowledge limits and a “did not know and should not reasonably have known” safe harbor within the defined term “traffics” in § 6023(13). As Justice Barrett and Justice Kavanaugh both emphasize, superadding a freestanding, global mens rea element to § 6082(a)(1)(A) would be atextual and would risk making the definition’s calibrated carveouts and notice mechanisms partly redundant. The criminal-law scienter cases (e.g., Rehaif/Staples/Liparota) do not carry the same weight in this civil, highly specified scheme; where Congress has expressly chosen how knowledge matters, our role is to enforce that choice rather than rewrite it. A narrow holding that liability turns on satisfying § 6023(13)’s definition (including its built-in knowledge-based exclusions) best preserves institutional legitimacy and keeps us on the text.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains the background presumption of scienter and attendant fair-notice concerns, but that canon cannot justify adding an atextual element where Congress has already specified how knowledge matters. As Justice Barrett explains, § 6023(13)’s unusually detailed definition of “traffics” contains the operative knowledge/intent language and explicit knowledge-based exclusions (including “did not know and should not reasonably have known”), so superadding a freestanding scienter requirement to § 6082(a)(1)(A) would create redundancy and revise the scheme. The Chief Justice’s distinction from Rehaif is persuasive: those cases turned on how “knowingly” grammatically modified elements in criminal prohibitions, whereas here Congress embedded the mens rea calibration in the incorporated definition. Under a textualist, original-public-meaning approach, our role is to apply the definition Congress enacted, not to impose an additional intent hurdle that Congress conspicuously omitted from the liability clause.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains the presumption of scienter and the fairness concern about sweeping in innocent commerce, but that presumption is substantially answered by the text Congress enacted. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, Congress placed the mens rea and notice calibration inside the defined term “traffics” in § 6023(13), including a “did not know and should not reasonably have known” exclusion; superadding a freestanding subjective-intent element onto § 6082(a)(1)(A) would be atextual and risk redundancy. Justice Kavanaugh’s Safeco analogy further supports treating this as a civil, highly specified scheme where Congress already chose the relevant knowledge standard, making criminal-case scienter presumptions like Rehaif comparatively weak. Practical consequences also cut against respondent’s overlay: an extra subjective-knowledge requirement would predictably invite willful blindness through intermediaries and frustrate the deterrent structure Congress designed.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The respondent’s best argument remains fair notice: civil liability for “trafficking” should not attach absent subjective knowledge, lest innocent commercial actors be swept in. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, Congress directly addressed that concern by embedding the knowledge calibration and safe harbors (including “did not know and should not reasonably have known”) within the defined term “traffics” in § 6023(13), so importing an additional, freestanding scienter element into § 6082(a)(1)(A) would be atextual and redundantly rewrite the statute’s architecture. Justice Kagan’s point reinforces the real-world stakes: a heightened subjective-intent requirement would predictably shift proof burdens onto victims least able to access internal corporate knowledge pre-discovery, undermining the remedial design Congress enacted. Criminal-law scienter precedents like Rehaif and Staples do not dislodge this reading because this is a civil scheme where Congress already specified where and how knowledge matters, and we should enforce that calibrated structure rather than add extra hurdles.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point remains the presumption of scienter to avoid unfair surprise in civil liability, but that presumption loses force where Congress affirmatively specified the knowledge calibration inside the definition of “traffics,” including the “did not know and should not reasonably have known” carveout and notice mechanisms. As Chief Justice Roberts stresses, reading § 6082(a)(1)(A) to add a freestanding mens rea would be atextual and would also distort workability by making Congress’s detailed exclusions partly redundant and shifting the statutory architecture from rule-and-exception to an extra element. Justice Barrett’s reliance on Safeco is helpful: in a civil scheme with express knowledge/notice features, we generally don’t overlay an additional, generalized scienter requirement from criminal-case presumptions like Rehaif. On a pragmatic textualist approach, the administrable and coherent reading is to enforce liability when conduct satisfies § 6023(13)’s definition (with its built-in culpability limits), not to invent another intent layer that Congress did not write.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point remains the presumption of scienter to avoid sweeping in innocents, but that canon cannot justify rewriting a statute that already calibrates culpability in the definition Congress chose to make dispositive. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett stress, § 6023(13) embeds knowledge and “should not reasonably have known” limits, plus notice mechanisms; superadding an independent “knowingly and intentionally” element to § 6082(a)(1)(A) would be atextual and would make those carveouts partly redundant. The Rehaif/Staples/Liparota line does not dislodge this because those cases turned on different grammatical cues—often in criminal statutes—whereas here Congress located the mental-state work in the defined term “traffics,” and our separation-of-powers role is to enforce that choice. Justice Kagan’s workability point reinforces the textual reading: shifting the burden into the plaintiff’s prima facie case via an implied scienter overlay would distort the scheme Congress enacted.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains the fair-notice/scienter presumption, but it does not justify superadding a freestanding subjective-knowledge element when Congress already calibrated mens rea and notice within the statutory definition of “traffics,” including the express “did not know, and should not have known” exclusion. Chief Justice Roberts’s structural point is persuasive: reading § 6082(a)(1)(A) to incorporate § 6023(13) as written avoids redundancy and respects a detailed scheme Congress enacted in a politically sensitive area, rather than rewriting it under a generalized presumption drawn mostly from criminal cases. Justice Barrett’s Safeco analogy reinforces that in civil statutes with explicit knowledge and reason-to-know standards, our precedent counsels restraint in importing broader scienter overlays. Nothing in colleagues’ cited cases (e.g., Rehaif/Staples) genuinely undermines this text-and-structure approach because those decisions turned on different grammatical cues and criminal-law default rules not present here.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The respondent’s best argument remains the presumption of scienter and fair-notice concerns, but the text and structure show Congress already addressed those concerns in the definition of “traffics” in § 6023(13), including its “knowingly and intentionally” formulation and express knowledge-based exclusions (including “did not know and should not reasonably have known”). As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, adding a freestanding, global scienter element to § 6082(a)(1)(A) would be an atextual superaddition that risks redundancy by displacing the calibrated carveouts and notice mechanisms Congress enacted. Justice Thomas’s Flores-Figueroa point is methodologically persuasive: we should not relocate knowledge language by inference when Congress has specified where it applies, especially in a civil scheme with unusually detailed definitional tailoring. Because the statute is not silent on mens rea and already builds in both actual-knowledge and reason-to-know limits, the generalized scienter presumption from criminal cases like Staples/Rehaif does not genuinely undermine the textual reading here.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest move—the scienter presumption drawn from cases like Rehaif—does not overcome this statute’s specific architecture, because Congress placed the key mental-state and fair-notice work inside the defined term “traffics” and its explicit exclusions (including “did not know and should not reasonably have known”). As Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett emphasize, adding a freestanding subjective-knowledge element to § 6082(a)(1)(A) would create redundancy and partially displace Congress’s calibrated notice-based carveouts, effectively rewriting a detailed civil remedial scheme. Justice Sotomayor’s practical point also matters to my procedural-fairness lens: requiring proof of a defendant’s internal, subjective intent as part of the prima facie case would predictably reward informational asymmetries at the pleading and pre-discovery stages and weaken the protection Congress enacted. Rehaif is distinguishable because it turned on how “knowingly” modified elements in a criminal prohibition; here Congress used a different drafting method by embedding scienter limits in the definition itself, so the better, administrable reading is to apply § 6023(13) as written.

John Roberts.reasoning: The better reading is that Congress defined the operative liability trigger—whether a person “traffics”—in 22 U.S.C. § 6023(13), and expressly embedded knowledge limitations and carveouts there (e.g., exclusions for persons who “did not know and should not have known” of the confiscation), rather than creating an additional, freestanding scienter element in § 6082(a)(1)(A). Imposing a separate requirement that a plaintiff prove the defendant subjectively knew and intended to traffic in confiscated property risks rewriting the statute and narrowing Congress’s chosen scheme, contrary to the ordinary interpretive approach of giving effect to the text and structure as enacted. To preserve institutional legitimacy and avoid a sweeping reconfiguration of a politically sensitive statute, the Court should decide narrowly: liability turns on satisfying the statutory definition of “traffics,” including its internal knowledge-related exclusions and notice features, without layering on an atextual mens rea element. This approach aligns with the Court’s reluctance to infer additional mental-state requirements where Congress has already specified how knowledge matters within the statutory framework (cf. Liparota and Staples’ emphasis on reading mens rea in light of statutory text and structure).

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of Title III creates liability for “any person” who “traffics” in confiscated property, 22 U.S.C. § 6082(a)(1)(A), and Congress placed the statute’s knowledge concepts in the defined term itself—particularly the “knows or should have known” language and related carveouts in 22 U.S.C. § 6023(13). Under a textualist reading, where Congress expressly specifies knowledge requirements and exceptions in a definition, courts may not graft an additional freestanding scienter element onto the cause of action; doing so violates the rule against atextual additions and effectively rewrites the statute. The proper inquiry is therefore whether the defendant’s conduct fits the statutory definition of “traffics” (including its knowledge-based exclusions), not whether the plaintiff separately proves subjective knowledge and intent beyond what the definition requires. This approach tracks the Court’s mens rea-modifier analysis in Flores-Figueroa v. United States, which emphasized adhering to how Congress attached knowledge language to particular statutory elements rather than inventing extra requirements.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The text of § 6082(a)(1)(A) imposes liability on “any person” who “traffics,” and Congress then defined “traffics” in § 6023(13) with specific knowledge-based limitations (e.g., exclusions where a person “did not know and had no reason to know” of the confiscation), as well as notice-related provisions—strong evidence Congress chose where and how to address scienter. Imposing an additional, freestanding requirement that plaintiffs prove subjective knowledge and intent to traffic is an atextual gloss that risks nullifying the statute’s carefully drafted carveouts and its deterrent remedial scheme. The Court’s ordinary approach is to respect Congress’s allocation of mental-state requirements in the statutory text and structure, rather than to add extra-elements by inference in a civil liability provision that already speaks to knowledge in its definitions and exceptions. Practically, the Eleventh Circuit’s heightened scienter rule would invite easy evasion through intermediaries and frustrate enforcement in a context where Congress plainly sought robust private remedies against commercial exploitation of confiscated property.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Title III’s text makes liability turn on whether a defendant “traffics” in confiscated property, and Congress placed knowledge concepts where it chose: inside the statutory definition of “traffics” and its carveouts in 22 U.S.C. § 6023(13), rather than as a freestanding element in § 6082(a)(1)(A). Reading an additional, atextual scienter element into the cause of action would dilute Congress’s remedial and deterrent design and, as a practical matter, would burden victims of confiscation—often with limited access to proof of corporate intent before discovery—while enabling sophisticated actors to insulate themselves through intermediaries. The better reading follows the statute’s structure and respects that when Congress specifies knowledge/notice limitations in definitional exclusions, courts should not add extra mens rea hurdles beyond the text. Unlike cases such as Rehaif v. United States, 139 S. Ct. 2191 (2019), where “knowingly” grammatically modified the offense provision, Helms-Burton places the relevant mental-state language within the definition of “traffics,” confirming Congress’s chosen allocation of proof.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 6082(a)(1)(A) creates liability for any person who “traffics,” and Congress then did the mens rea work in the definition of “traffics” in § 6023(13), including express knowledge-based limitations (e.g., exclusions where a person lacked and had no reason to know, and the statute’s notice-related mechanisms). Reading an additional, freestanding “knowingly and intentionally” element into the cause of action risks making those embedded carveouts and notice provisions partly redundant and undermining statutory coherence. Where Congress has spoken to knowledge in specific definitional exclusions, courts should be reluctant to infer a broader scienter overlay that Congress did not include in the liability clause—especially in a civil statute with a detailed, workable scheme. That approach also aligns with this Court’s caution in Global-Tech Appliances, Inc. v. SEB S.A. against judicially reengineering mens rea when the statute’s text and structure already specify how knowledge operates.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The cause of action imposes liability on “any person” who “traffics” in confiscated property, § 6082(a)(1)(A), and Congress supplied a detailed definition of “traffics” in § 6023(13) that already builds in knowledge-related limitations (including exclusions for persons who “did not know, and should not reasonably have known” of the confiscation). Reading an additional freestanding scienter element (knowledge and intent) into § 6082(a)(1)(A) would be atextual and would violate the ordinary rule that courts do not add mens rea requirements where Congress has specified the mental-state work it wants done elsewhere in the statute. The better reading—consistent with expressio unius and separation-of-powers principles—is that plaintiffs must prove trafficking as Congress defined it, while defendants may invoke the statute’s express knowledge-based carveouts and other exceptions where applicable rather than courts inventing a new element.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The best reading of Title III follows Congress’s textual choices: § 6082(a)(1)(A) imposes liability on any person who “traffics,” and § 6023(13) defines “traffics” to include certain “knowingly and intentionally” commercial dealings while also embedding specific knowledge-based exclusions (e.g., where a person “did not know, and should not have known” of the confiscation). Where Congress has placed mens rea language inside a defined term and paired it with express carveouts, courts should not add a freestanding, atextual scienter element beyond the definition—especially given the statute’s workability and notice structure (including the Act’s notice provisions) that already calibrate culpability. This differs from Rehaif v. United States, which turned on the placement of “knowingly” modifying a criminal prohibition’s elements; here, Congress did not use a global “knowingly violates” formulation and instead located knowledge requirements precisely in the “traffics” definition. Respecting that structure adheres to judicial restraint, preserves predictability, and avoids courts rewriting a politically sensitive statute under the guise of interpretation.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The cause of action in 22 U.S.C. § 6082(a)(1)(A) turns on whether a person “traffics” in confiscated property, and Congress supplied an unusually detailed, operative definition of “traffics” in 22 U.S.C. § 6023(13) that itself embeds knowledge concepts through express exclusions (e.g., where a person “did not know and should not reasonably have known” of the confiscation) and notice-related provisions. That structure is strong textual evidence that Congress calibrated mens rea where it wanted it—inside the definition and carveouts—so courts should not superadd a freestanding, atextual requirement of subjective knowledge and intent as an element of liability. The general presumption of scienter (seen in cases like Staples v. United States and Liparota v. United States) is least persuasive here because those cases addressed criminal statutes or otherwise ambiguous liability terms, whereas Title III is a civil cause of action with an explicit, knowledge-sensitive definitional scheme that would be partially redundant if an extra scienter element were implied. Safeco Ins. Co. of Am. v. Burr likewise supports respecting Congress’s chosen textual placement of scienter-like limitations in a civil statute rather than rewriting the cause of action to require more than the statute says.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Title III makes civil liability turn on whether a defendant “traffics” in confiscated property, 22 U.S.C. § 6082(a)(1)(A), and Congress embedded the relevant knowledge limitations in the definition of “traffics” itself and its express carveouts (including exclusions for conduct undertaken without knowledge or reason to know), 22 U.S.C. § 6023(13). Reading an additional, freestanding “knowingly and intentionally” scienter element into § 6082(a)(1)(A) risks displacing those textual notice-based safeguards and invites courts to rewrite a detailed statutory scheme, undermining procedural fairness by allowing defendants to avoid liability through informational asymmetries prior to discovery. This interpretation also best respects Congress’s remedial and deterrent design—targeting commercial exploitation of confiscated property—while leaving fair-notice concerns to the statute’s own knowledge-related exclusions and to ordinary due-process constraints. To the extent standing is raised, TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez confirms courts must ensure a concrete injury, but it does not negate Congress’s ability to define and remedy a concrete, particularized invasion of a property-related interest alleged here.
